Apoptosis. It is programmed cell death, a controlled process in which a cell disassembles itself in response to signals, without damaging neighboring cells through inflammation. Unlike necrosis, which is traumatic cell death, apoptosis is an organized, energy-dependent process involving the activation of proteases called caspases and endonucleases, DNA fragmentation, and membrane blebbing. Essential for development, immune function, and preventing cancer, apoptosis is triggered by DNA damage checkpoints, growth-factor withdrawal, or external stressors.

There are two main pathways. The intrinsic or mitochondrial pathway is triggered by DNA damage, oxidative stress, or growth-factor withdrawal. During this pathway, p fifty-three activates pro-apoptotic Bcl-two family members Bax and Bak. Mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization, or MOMP, releases cytochrome c into the cytoplasm. Cytochrome c binds Apaf-one, recruiting procaspase-nine into the apoptosome complex. The extrinsic or death-receptor pathway operates differently. Ligands like TNF-alpha, FasL, or TRAIL bind death receptors on the cell surface and recruit adaptor proteins that directly activate caspase-eight.

Executioner caspases—caspase-three, six, and seven—cleave hundreds of protein substrates, disassembling the nuclear lamina, condensing chromatin, and fragmenting DNA into pieces approximately one hundred eighty base pairs long. Hallmark features of apoptosis include cell shrinkage, membrane blebbing where the surface bulges, chromatin condensation and fragmentation, phosphatidylserine externalization which signals "eat me," and the formation of apoptotic bodies. Phagocytes recognize phosphatidylserine on apoptotic cell surfaces and engulf intact cells without rupturing membranes, preventing inflammatory cytokine release and keeping the process immunologically silent.

Apoptosis is critical during development, particularly in digit sculpting where webbing is removed, elimination of interdigital tissue, and matching neuron number to targets through survival factor competition. Cancer cells evade apoptosis via p fifty-three mutations that lose sensor function, Bcl-two overexpression that blocks cytochrome c release, or caspase pathway deletions. Therapeutically, chemotherapy and radiation kill cancer cells partly by triggering apoptosis, while BCL-two inhibitors and death-receptor agonists restore apoptosis in resistant cancers. Dysregulation presents problems in both directions—insufficient apoptosis in cancer and autoimmunity, excessive apoptosis in neurodegeneration, AIDS, and ischemic injury. Understanding apoptosis opened new drug development approaches.
